subjective.topic: Taxation Basics and Fiscal Policy
subjective.question: Define "tax". Also give its statutory definition under the Income Tax Ordinance 2001.
subjective.answer: The literal meanings of tax are "burden" and "strain". The general definition of tax is: general compulsory contributions of wealth levied upon persons by the state, to meet the expenses incurred in providing common benefits upon the residents. The statutory definition is: tax means any tax imposed under Chapter II of the Income Tax Ordinance 2001, and includes a penalty, fee or other charge or any sum or amount leviable or payable under the Ordinance.

subjective.topic: Taxation Basics and Fiscal Policy
subjective.question: Differentiate between tax and fee.
subjective.answer: Tax is a compulsory levy and it is the legal obligation of the person to pay the amount of tax required under the law; the taxpayer cannot claim any direct benefit in return for the tax paid. Payment of a fee, on the other hand, is at the discretion of a person, and when a fee is paid the person becomes entitled to claim counter benefits (a specific service) in return. This entitlement of counter benefit is the main difference between a tax and a fee.

subjective.topic: Taxation Basics and Fiscal Policy
subjective.question: What is fiscal policy? Discuss its objectives and instruments.
subjective.answer: Fiscal policy is a discipline that deals with the arrangements adopted by the government to collect revenue and make expenditures, so that social and economic stability could be attained and maintained. Its objectives are: economic development; raising the level of employment (achieving full employment level); influencing consumption patterns; price stability; redistribution of income; and removal of deficit in the Balance of Payments. Its instruments are: government expenditures, taxes, deficit financing, subsidies and transfer payments, like unemployment allowances.

subjective.topic: Taxation Basics and Fiscal Policy
subjective.question: Explain the canons of taxation.
subjective.answer: The canons of taxation are: (1) Simplicity - the taxation system should be plain and easily understandable by the taxpayer. (2) Convenience - the time of payment and mode of collection should be convenient for the taxpayer as well as the tax collector. (3) Certainty - the amount of payment should be certain and there should be no arbitrariness or ambiguity in respect of the amount of tax to be paid. (4) Judicious - the system should be based on equity, fair play and the principles of natural justice. (5) Capacity to Pay - tax should be levied keeping in view the capacity to sacrifice of the person; those with more income should pay at higher rates and those with low income at lower rates. (6) Benefit Principle - taxes should be levied according to the benefits derived by the person from the state. (7) Business Friendly - the taxation policy should boost the business atmosphere and not discourage the investment environment.

subjective.topic: Taxation Basics and Fiscal Policy
subjective.question: What is taxation management? State its essentials.
subjective.answer: Taxation management is a strategy whereby a person manages his business and other transactions and activities in such a way so as to make maximum use of tax holidays, exemptions, concessions, rebates, tax credits and deductible allowances available under the law, and as a result is able to derive the benefit of minimizing his tax liability. Its essentials are: understanding and application of updated laws, particularly tax laws, rules and procedures; application and use of benefits such as tax credits, rebates, exemptions and reductions available under the law; maintenance of records and books of account as per the requirements of law; and disclosure of true facts, i.e., there should be no concealment in furnishing information or preparing accounts and data.

subjective.topic: Taxation Basics and Fiscal Policy
subjective.question: Explain the different types of taxes.
subjective.answer: The main types of taxes are: (1) Direct taxes - taxes where the incidence of taxation is on the person on whom they are levied, e.g., income tax. (2) Indirect taxes - taxes where the incidence of tax can be shifted by the person on whom they are levied to other persons, e.g., sales tax. (3) Proportional taxes - taxes levied at the same percentage on all taxpayers, e.g., sales tax levied at a flat rate. (4) Progressive taxes - based on the capacity to pay principle; the rate of tax increases as the income increases. (5) Regressive taxes - the opposite of progressive taxes; the rate of tax decreases as the income increases. (6) Value Added Tax (VAT) - a tax paid to the government on goods and services, which can be reclaimed by the retailers in the chain.

subjective.topic: The Income Tax Ordinance 2001: Structure, Interpretation and Definitions
subjective.question: Describe the scheme (structure) of the Income Tax Ordinance 2001.
subjective.answer: The scheme of the Income Tax Ordinance 2001 is as follows: there are thirteen chapters; the chapters are divided into parts and divisions; there are 240 sections; and the Ordinance comprises of seven schedules, which are an integral part of the Ordinance. The Income Tax Rules 2002 were promulgated by the CBR on 1st July 2002, in exercise of the powers granted under section 237 of the Ordinance.

subjective.topic: The Income Tax Ordinance 2001: Structure, Interpretation and Definitions
subjective.question: Differentiate between exclusive (exhaustive) and inclusive definitions, with examples from section 2 of the Ordinance.
subjective.answer: An exclusive or exhaustive definition starts with the expression "mean" or "means" and excludes the ordinary dictionary meanings of the word. Examples: section 2(2) "Appellate Tribunal", 2(5A) "assessment year", 2(6) "association of persons", 2(13) "Commissioner" and 2(15) "debt". An inclusive definition starts with the expression "includes" and includes the dictionary meanings as well as the meanings conveyed by the definition. Examples: section 2(9) "business", 2(22) "employment" and section 11A "charitable purpose". Some definitions are exclusive as well as inclusive, containing both elements, e.g., section 2(7) "banking company" and section 2(41) "permanent establishment".

subjective.topic: The Income Tax Ordinance 2001: Structure, Interpretation and Definitions
subjective.question: What are the internal aids to the interpretation of a statute?
subjective.answer: Internal aids are those aids which are available within the Act itself. They include: the explanation to a section; marginal notes; punctuation marks; the preamble; the title of a chapter; the non-obstante clause; the proviso; and the context of the statute.

subjective.topic: Tax Year, Persons and Accounting Methods
subjective.question: What is a tax year? Differentiate between a normal tax year and a special tax year.
subjective.answer: A tax year is a period of twelve months for tax purposes. The normal tax year starts on 1st July and ends on 30th June following; the tax year of a salaried person is the normal tax year. A special tax year is a different accounting period adopted by a person after seeking approval from the Commissioner under section 74(3). Examples of special accounting years are: all insurance companies and persons exporting rice - 1st January to 31st December; companies manufacturing sugar - 1st October to 30th September; and persons carrying on cotton ginning, rice husking and oil milling - 1st September to 31st August.

subjective.topic: Tax Year, Persons and Accounting Methods
subjective.question: Determine the tax years relating to the following accounting periods: (i) Mr. Aslam, a rice exporter: 1st January 2008 to 31st December 2008; (ii) Mr. Kamal, a manufacturer of shawls: 1st April 2008 to 31st March 2009; (iii) M/S XYZ, a company manufacturing sugar: 1st October 2007 to 30th September 2008.
subjective.answer: All three are special tax years. The tax year is the normal tax year (1st July to 30th June) in which the special accounting period ends. (i) The period ends on 31st December 2008, which falls in the normal tax year 2009 - Special Tax Year 2009. (ii) The period ends on 31st March 2009, which also falls in the normal tax year 2009 - Special Tax Year 2009. (iii) The period ends on 30th September 2008, which falls in the normal tax year 2009 - Special Tax Year 2009.

subjective.topic: Tax Year, Persons and Accounting Methods
subjective.question: Give the legal status of the following under section 80 of the Income Tax Ordinance 2001: (a) Al-Habib Bank Limited; (b) Mr. Z, a director in a private company; (c) Punjab University; (d) Mr. A & B, joint owners of a building.
subjective.answer: (a) Al-Habib Bank Limited is a Banking Company. (b) Mr. Z, a director in a private company, is an Individual. (c) Punjab University is a Company. (d) Mr. A & B, being joint owners of a building, form an Association of Persons (AOP), because an association of persons includes a firm, a Hindu Undivided Family, any artificial juridical person and any body of persons formed under a foreign law, but does not include a company.

subjective.topic: Tax Year, Persons and Accounting Methods
subjective.question: Explain the methods of accounting under section 32 of the Income Tax Ordinance 2001.
subjective.answer: Under section 32, income chargeable to tax under the head "Income from Business" is computed on the cash basis or the accrual basis, in accordance with the method of accounting regularly employed by the person. For companies, the accrual basis method of accounting is compulsory under section 32(2). Other persons, such as individuals, firms and sole proprietors, are free to choose any kind of base. A change of the method of accounting can be made under section 32(4). Under the cash basis, income is charged when received and expenses are allowed when paid; under the accrual basis, income is charged when it becomes due or receivable and expenses are allowed when they are incurred or become payable.

subjective.topic: Tax Year, Persons and Accounting Methods
subjective.question: A firm ABC, maintaining its accounts on accrual basis, is entitled to receive Rs. 10,000 on 27th June 2008, but the actual payment is made on 01 August 2008. In which tax year would the amount be charged to tax? What would be the position if the firm maintained its accounts on cash basis?
subjective.answer: Under the accrual basis, the amount would be charged to tax in tax year 2008, because under this basis income is taxed when it accrues or becomes receivable, and the entitlement arose on 27th June 2008, which falls in tax year 2008 (1st July 2007 to 30th June 2008); the date of actual receipt is irrelevant. Under the cash basis, the amount would be charged to tax in tax year 2009, because under this basis income is taxed when it is actually received, and the payment was received on 01 August 2008, which falls in tax year 2009.

subjective.topic: Scope of Income, Heads of Income and Agriculture Income
subjective.question: What are the heads of income under section 11 of the Income Tax Ordinance 2001?
subjective.answer: Under section 11, the sources of income are classified into five heads: (1) Salary (section 12); (2) Income from Property (section 15); (3) Income from Business (section 18); (4) Capital Gains (section 37); and (5) Income from Other Sources (section 39). The total income of a person for a tax year is computed by taking into account the amounts chargeable under each of these heads. It is important to note that no deductions are allowed in computing income under the head "Salary".

subjective.topic: Scope of Income, Heads of Income and Agriculture Income
subjective.question: Define agricultural income under section 41. How is partly agricultural and partly non-agricultural income treated?
subjective.answer: Under section 41, agricultural income means: any rent or revenue derived by a person from land which is situated in Pakistan and is used for agricultural purposes; any income derived by a person from such land from agriculture; any income derived by a person from the performance of a process ordinarily employed by a cultivator or receiver of rent-in-kind to render the produce raised or received by him fit to be taken to market; and any income derived from a building owned and occupied by the cultivator or receiver of rent-in-kind in connection with such land. Human effort on the land is the factor that distinguishes agricultural from non-agricultural income, and agricultural income is exempt from tax. Where income is partly agricultural and partly non-agricultural - for example, a sugar mill that grows its own sugarcane and manufactures sugar, or a person who grows tea leaves and manufactures tea - the agricultural part remains exempt, while the manufacturing part is chargeable to tax under the head "Income from Business"; in computing that part, the market value of the agricultural produce utilized as raw material is deducted, and no further deduction is allowed for expenditure incurred as a cultivator or receiver of rent-in-kind.

subjective.topic: Scope of Income, Heads of Income and Agriculture Income
subjective.question: What is deemed income? Give an example. Also explain the tax treatment of lump sum receipts.
subjective.answer: Deemed income is an amount which is not the real income of a person in the ordinary sense but is treated as income for the purposes of taxation. For example, a cash gift received by a person is treated as his deemed income, whereas a gift received through a proper (banking) transaction is not treated as deemed income. Lump sum receipts are amounts received in one go instead of periodically, such as commuted pension, provident fund receipts and golden handshake payments; they are chargeable to tax. In the case of a lump sum receipt like golden handshake, the taxpayer can opt, with the approval of the Commissioner, to be charged at the average tax rate of the last three years instead of the current tax rate.

subjective.topic: Scope of Income, Heads of Income and Agriculture Income
subjective.question: What is clubbing of income? What is its effect on tax liability?
subjective.answer: Clubbing of income means the association or combination of the income of one person, or of more than one head of income, with the income of another person for the purpose of taxation, instead of taxing that income separately in the hands of the person who earned it. The effect of clubbing is that the combined income becomes larger and falls in a higher bracket, so a higher bracket rate of tax is charged on it.

subjective.topic: Exemptions and Tax Concessions
subjective.question: What are exemptions and tax concessions? Explain the kinds of concessions provided in the Second Schedule to the Ordinance.
subjective.answer: Exemptions and tax concessions are dealt with in Part VII of Chapter III (sections 41 to 53) of the Income Tax Ordinance 2001 and in the Second Schedule, which is governed by section 53. The Second Schedule provides three kinds of relief: Part I provides exemptions, under which specified incomes are wholly exempt from tax, e.g., income of the Fund for Promotion of Science and Technology in Pakistan and donations to certain approved institutions. Part II provides reduction in tax rates, e.g., the presumptive tax charged at 8% of gross receipts from the shipping business of a non-resident person, and profit on Special US Dollar Bonds taxed at the rate of 10%. Part III provides reduction in tax liability, e.g., the tax liability of a senior citizen aged 60 years or above, whose taxable income does not exceed Rs. 500,000, is reduced by 50%.

subjective.topic: Exemptions and Tax Concessions
subjective.question: State the conditions under which the salary of an employee of a foreign government is exempt under section 43. Is the salary of such an employee, who is a citizen of Pakistan, exempt from tax?
subjective.answer: Under section 43, any salary received by an employee of a foreign government for services rendered to such government is exempt from tax provided that: (a) the employee is a citizen of the foreign country and not a citizen of Pakistan; (b) the services performed by the employee are of a character similar to those performed by employees of the Federal Government in foreign countries; and (c) the foreign government grants a similar exemption to employees of the Federal Government performing similar services in that country. Since the first condition is not satisfied in the case of an employee who is a citizen of Pakistan, his salary is not exempt; it is wholly taxable.

subjective.topic: Residential Status and Geographical Source of Income
subjective.question: Explain the residential status of an individual under section 82, including the rules for counting the days of stay.
subjective.answer: Under section 82, an individual shall be a resident individual for a tax year if: (a) he is present in Pakistan for a period of, or periods amounting in aggregate to, one hundred and eighty-three days or more in the tax year; or (b) he is an employee or official of the Federal Government or a Provincial Government posted abroad in the tax year. The rules for counting days are: a part of a day is counted as a whole day, for example the day of arrival or the day of departure; and the following days are counted as whole days - a public holiday, a day of leave including sick leave, a day on which the individual's activity is stopped because of a strike etc., and a holiday spent in Pakistan.

subjective.topic: Residential Status and Geographical Source of Income
subjective.question: Mr. Kishan Kumar, during his yearly tour in Pakistan, spends 155 working days, 26 off-working days, 1 strike day and 1 public holiday in a tax year 2008-09. Determine his residential status.
subjective.answer: The total period of his stay in Pakistan is 155 + 26 + 1 + 1 = 183 days. Under the rules governing resident individuals, a public holiday, a day of leave and a day on which activity is stopped because of a strike are all counted as whole days. His presence in Pakistan therefore amounts to 183 days, which is not less than the minimum of 183 days required under section 82. Hence, Mr. Kishan Kumar is a Resident Individual for the tax year 2008-09.

subjective.topic: Residential Status and Geographical Source of Income
subjective.question: Explain the residential status of a company and of an association of persons under the Ordinance.
subjective.answer: A company is a resident company for a tax year if it is incorporated or formed by or under any law in force in Pakistan, or the control and management of its affairs is situated wholly in Pakistan at any time in the year, or it is a Provincial Government or a local authority in Pakistan (section 83). Therefore, a company incorporated under the Companies Ordinance 1984 remains a resident company even if most of its branches and the control and management of its affairs are situated outside Pakistan, because a body corporate formed by or under the law of Pakistan is treated as a resident company. An association of persons is a resident AOP for a tax year if the control and management of the affairs of the association is situated wholly or partly in Pakistan at any time in the year (section 84).

subjective.topic: Residential Status and Geographical Source of Income
subjective.question: Differentiate between Pakistan-source income and foreign-source income, giving examples. Also state the scope of total income of a resident and a non-resident person.
subjective.answer: Pakistan-source income (section 101) includes, among others: salary paid by, or on behalf of, the Federal Government, a Provincial Government or a local authority in Pakistan, wherever the employment is exercised; rental income derived from the lease of immovable property in Pakistan; royalty paid by a resident person; dividend paid by a resident company; any gain arising on the disposal of shares in a resident company; and business income derived from a business carried on in Pakistan, including sales of goods in Pakistan through a permanent establishment. Foreign-source income is income that is not Pakistan-source income, e.g., salary received for services rendered abroad to a foreign employer, income from property situated outside Pakistan, and gain on the disposal of shares in a non-resident company. Under section 11(5), the income of a resident person is computed by taking into account both Pakistan-source income and foreign-source income, whereas under section 11(6) a non-resident person is charged to tax only on Pakistan-source income.

subjective.topic: Residential Status and Geographical Source of Income
subjective.question: Define "permanent establishment" under section 2(41). What does not fall within its ambit? Also state the relation between a non-resident person and its permanent establishment under section 105.
subjective.answer: In relation to a person, "permanent establishment" means a fixed place of business through which the business of the person is wholly or partly carried on, and includes: a place of management, branch office, factory or workshop, premises for soliciting orders, warehouse, permanent sales exhibition or sales outlet; a mine, oil or gas well, quarry or any other place of extraction of natural resources; a building site, construction, assembly or installation project continuing for a period exceeding ninety days; and an agent who habitually exercises authority to conclude contracts on behalf of the person. A liaison office does not come under the ambit of a permanent establishment, except where the office engages in the negotiation of contracts other than contracts of purchase. Under section 105, the profit of the permanent establishment is computed on the basis that it is a distinct and separate person (a separate legal entity) engaged in the same or similar activities under the same or similar conditions and dealing wholly independently with the non-resident person of which it is a permanent establishment.

subjective.topic: Residential Status and Geographical Source of Income
subjective.question: Define "royalty" under section 2(54) of the Ordinance.
subjective.answer: "Royalty" means any amount paid or payable, however described or computed, whether periodical or lump sum, as consideration for: (a) the use of, or the right to use, any patent, invention, design or model, secret formula or process, or trademark, or any other similar property or right; (b) the use of, or the right to use, any copyright of a literary, artistic or scientific work, including films or video tapes for use in connection with television, or tapes in connection with radio broadcasting; (c) the supply of any technical, industrial, commercial or scientific knowledge, experience or skill; (d) the use of, or the right to use, any industrial, commercial or scientific equipment; or (e) the reception of, or the right to receive, any visual images or sounds transmitted by satellite, cable or optic fibre.

subjective.topic: Residential Status and Geographical Source of Income
subjective.question: Explain the treatment of foreign-source salary of a resident individual under section 102, and the exemption available to short-term resident individuals under section 50.
subjective.answer: Under section 102, any foreign-source salary received by a resident individual shall be exempt from tax if the individual has paid foreign income tax in respect of the salary; if no foreign tax has been paid on it, the salary remains chargeable to tax in Pakistan. Under section 50, the foreign-source income of a short-term resident individual - that is, an individual who is a resident individual solely by reason of his employment and who is present in Pakistan for a period or periods not exceeding three years - is exempt from tax under the Ordinance.

subjective.topic: Income from Salary
subjective.question: What is "salary" under section 12? Why is an amount received by a member of an AOP from the AOP not taxed under the head "Salary"?
subjective.answer: Under section 12(2), "salary" means any amount received by an employee from any employment, whether of a revenue or capital nature, including wages, salary, leave pay, overtime payment, bonus, commission, fees, gratuity, pension, perquisites and amounts received as consideration for entering into or terminating employment. Under section 2(22), "employment" includes a directorship or any other office involved in the management of a company, a position entitling the holder to a fixed or ascertainable remuneration, and the holding or acting in any public office. However, an amount received by a member of an association of persons from the AOP is not salary, because the member is not an employee of the AOP; the amount is treated as an appropriation of the profit of the AOP and is charged to tax under the head "Income from Business".

subjective.topic: Income from Salary
subjective.question: What are perquisites? How are the following valued under section 13: (a) services of a driver and gardener provided by the employer; (b) utilities provided by the employer; (c) a loan given by the employer at a concessional rate?
subjective.answer: Perquisites are the benefits, whether convertible into money or not, provided by an employer to an employee in addition to salary; their value, determined in accordance with section 13, is included in the employee's income chargeable under the head "Salary". (a) Where the services of a housekeeper, driver, gardener or other domestic assistant are provided by the employer, the total salary paid to such servant in the year for services rendered to the employee is added to the employee's salary, as reduced by any payment made by the employee to the employer for such services. (b) Where utilities (electricity, gas, water and telephone) are provided by the employer, the fair market value of the utilities provided is added to the employee's salary, as reduced by any payment made by the employee for the utilities. (c) Where the employer gives a loan on which no profit is payable, or profit is payable at a rate less than the benchmark rate (11% per annum for tax year 2009), the amount added to salary is the profit computed at the benchmark rate, or the difference between the profit computed at the benchmark rate and the profit actually paid by the employee, as the case may be.

subjective.topic: Income from Salary
subjective.question: How are the following amounts treated in computing gross total income? (a) Mr. A, a non-resident of Pakistan, receives interest of Rs. 100,000 on Australian Bonds, half of the amount being received in Pakistan. (b) Mr. A, a resident of Pakistan, receives the same interest. (c) Mr. X, a resident of Pakistan, receives a remittance of Rs. 20,000 from the UK out of past profits.
subjective.answer: (a) A non-resident person is charged to tax on Pakistan-source income; foreign-source income is chargeable in his hands only to the extent it is received in Pakistan. Interest on Australian Bonds is foreign-source income, so only the half received in Pakistan, i.e., Rs. 50,000, will be added in his gross total income. (b) A resident person is charged to tax on both Pakistan-source and foreign-source income (his worldwide income), so the full amount of Rs. 100,000 will be added in his gross total income, regardless of where it is received. (c) A remittance is not income; it is merely a transfer of money from one place to another. The remittance of Rs. 20,000 received out of past profits is therefore not included in the gross total income of Mr. X.
